title: Wisdom in the writings after Jesus
source_text: Ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ μετὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν γεγραμμένα ἔλθῃς βιβλία, εὕροις ἂν τοὺς μὲν ὄχλους τῶν πιστευόντων τῶν παραβολῶν ἀκούοντας ὡς ἔξω τυγχάνοντας καὶ ἀξίους μόνον τῶν ἐξωτερικῶν λόγων. τοὺς δὲ μαθητὰς κατ᾿ ἰδίαν τῶν παραβολῶν μανθάνοντας τὰς διηγήσεις· „κατ᾿ ἰδίαν“ γὰρ „τοῖς ἰδίοις μαθηταῖς ἐπέλυεν ἅπαντα“ ὁ Ἰησοῦς. προτιμῶν παρὰ τοὺς ὄχλους τοὺς τῆς σοφίας αὐτοῦ ἐπιδικαζομένους. ἐπαγγέλλεται δὲ τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν πιστεύουσι πέμψαι „σοφοὺς καὶ γραμματεῖς“ λέγων· „ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστελῶ εἰς ὑμᾶς σοφοὺς καὶ γραμματεῖς, καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀποκτενοῦσι καὶ σταυρώσουσι.“ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος δ᾿ ἐν τῷ καταλόγῳ τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ διδομένων χαρισμάτων πρῶτον ἔταξε τὸν λόγον τῆς σοφίας καὶ δεύτερον, ὡς ὑποβεβηκότα παρ᾿ ἐκεῖνον, τὸν λόγον τῆς γνώσεως τρίτον δέ που καὶ κατωτέρω τὴν πίστιν. καὶ ἐπεὶ τὸν λόγον προετίμα τῶν τεραστίων ἐνεργειῶν, διὰ τοῦτ᾿ „ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων“ καὶ „χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων“ ἐν τῇ κατωτέρω τίθησι χώρᾳ παρὰ τὰ λογικὰ χαρίσματα. μαρτυρεῖ δὲ τῇ Μωϋσέως πολυμαθείᾳ ὁ ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων Στέφανος, πάντως ἀπὸ τῶν παλαιῶν καὶ μὴ εἰς πολλοὺς ἐφθακότων γραμμάτων λαβών· φησὶ γάρ· „καὶ ἐπαιδεύθη Μωϋσῆς ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ Αἰγυπτίων.“ διὰ τοῦτο δὲ καὶ ἐν τοῖς τεραστίοις ὑπενοεῖτο, μή ποτ᾿ οὐ κατὰ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ θεόθεν ἥκειν ἐποίει αὐτὰ ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὰ Αἰγυπτίων μαθήματα, σοφὸς ὢν ἐν αὐτοῖς. τοιαῦτα γὰρ ὑπονοῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκάλεσε τοὺς ἐπαοιδοὺς τῶν Αἰγυπτίων καὶ τοὺς σοφιστὰς καὶ τοὺς φαρμακεῖς, οἵτινες ἠλέγχθησαν τὸ οὐδὲν ὄντες ὡς πρὸς τὴν ἐν Μωϋσεῖ σοφίαν ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν Αἰγυπτίων σοφίαν.
pass_a_gloss: And if you come also to the books written after Jesus, you would find the crowds (ὄχλοι) of those believing hearing the parables (παραβολαί) as being outside (ἔξω) and worthy only of the outer (ἐξωτερικοί) words (λόγοι), but the disciples (μαθηταί) learning (μανθάνω) privately (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν) the expositions (διηγήσεις) of the parables; for ‘privately to his own disciples he explained (ἐπιλύω) all things’ Jesus, honouring before (προτιμάω) the crowds those laying claim (ἐπιδικάζομαι) to his wisdom. And he promises (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to those believing in him to send ‘wise men and scribes (γραμματεῖς),’ saying: ‘Behold I will send (ἀποστέλλω) to you wise men and scribes, and of them they will kill (ἀποκτείνω) and crucify (σταυρόω).’ And Paul in the catalogue (κατάλογος) of the gifts (χαρίσματα) given by God placed (τάσσω) first the word of wisdom and second, as having stepped below (ὑποβαίνω) it, the word of knowledge (γνῶσις), and third somewhere also lower (κατωτέρω) faith (πίστις). And since he honoured the word before the wonder-working (τεράστιος) operations (ἐνέργειαι), for this ‘operations of powers (ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων)’ and ‘gifts of healings (ἰάματα)’ he places in the lower place (χώρα) beside the rational/verbal (λογικά) gifts. And Stephen in the Acts of the apostles bears witness (μαρτυρέω) to the much-learning (πολυμάθεια) of Moses, surely (πάντως) having taken [it] from ancient writings and not having reached (φθάνω) to many; for he says: ‘and Moses was educated (παιδεύω) in all wisdom of Egyptians.’ For this also in the wonders (τεράστια) he was suspected (ὑπονοέω), lest perhaps (μή ποτε) not according to the profession (ἐπαγγελία) of having come from God (θεόθεν ἥκειν) he did them but according to the learnings (μαθήματα) of Egyptians, being wise in them. For suspecting such things about him the king called the enchanters (ἐπαοιδοί) of the Egyptians and the sophists (σοφισταί) and the sorcerers (φαρμακεῖς), who were exposed (ἐλέγχω) as being nothing (τὸ οὐδέν) in relation to the wisdom in Moses beyond all wisdom of Egyptians.
pass_b_english: If you go on to the books written after Jesus as well, you would find that the crowds of believers hear the parables as those who are outside (Mark 4:11) and worthy only of the outward teachings, while the disciples learn privately the explanations of the parables. For Jesus “privately explained everything to his own disciples” (Mark 4:34), honouring above the crowds those who laid claim to his wisdom. He promises to those who believe in him that he will send “wise men and scribes,” saying: “See, I will send you wise men and scribes, and some of them they will kill and crucify” (Matthew 23:34).

Paul too, in his list of the gifts given by God, placed first the word of wisdom; second, as ranking below it, the word of knowledge; and third, lower still, faith (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). And because he valued the word above miraculous workings, he therefore sets “workings of powers” and “gifts of healings” in a lower place than the gifts of the word (1 Corinthians 12:9–10).

Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles, bears witness to the wide learning of Moses, no doubt taking this from ancient writings that had not reached many; for he says: “And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22). For this reason it was also suspected that he might be working his wonders not, as he professed, because he had come from God, but by the learning of the Egyptians, in which he was wise. For it was because he suspected something of this kind about him that the king called the enchanters of the Egyptians, and the wise men, and the sorcerers (Exodus 7:11); and they were proved to be nothing compared with the wisdom in Moses, which surpassed all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

choices.choice: ‘as those who are outside’ (ὡς ἔξω τυγχάνοντας) alludes to Mark 4:11 (τοῖς ἔξω ἐν παραβολαῖς), cited inline. The quoted ‘privately explained everything to his own disciples’ is Mark 4:34. Matthew 23:34 is quoted with Origen's own wording: future ἀποστελῶ, no ‘prophets’, and third-person ‘they will kill and crucify’ where the Gospel has the second person; in Matthew the words are spoken to scribes and Pharisees, while Origen presents them as a promise to believers. The English follows Origen. 1 Corinthians 12:8–10: word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith (12:8–9); gifts of healings and workings of powers (12:9–10); Origen names the last two in reverse order. τὰ λογικὰ χαρίσματα rendered ‘the gifts of the word’ to keep Origen's link with λόγος (it could also mean ‘gifts of reason’). κατὰ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ θεόθεν ἥκειν: ἐπαγγελία taken as ‘profession, claim’ (‘as he professed, because he had come from God’), not ‘promise’. The king's summoning of enchanters, wise men and sorcerers follows Exodus 7:11 (LXX σοφισταί, φαρμακοί, ἐπαοιδοί); their failure is narrated at Exodus 8:18–19, a possible further allusion left uncited. ‘ancient writings that had not reached many’ is Origen's conjecture about Stephen's source; no Scripture is meant. Reviewer: μή ποτ᾿ after ὑπενοεῖτο is rendered ‘that he might be’, which carries the hedge without the earlier stiff ‘of performing them perhaps not’.

Recast the stiff suspicion clause (ὑπενοεῖτο, μή ποτ᾿ οὐ … ἀλλά …) as ‘it was also suspected that he might be working his wonders not, as he professed, … but by the learning of the Egyptians, in which he was wise’
Checked Mark 4:11, Mark 4:34, Matthew 23:34, 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, Acts 7:22, Exodus 7:11; no other change
